h: A new foundation for Muslim politics: not Akbar, but the weaver of Banaras
dek: According to Ajay Gudavarthy, the politics of a single Muslim identity has failed, and the way forward lies in a shared struggle across caste and class.
body: Ajay Gudavarthy, who teaches political science at JNU, says the usual answer to rising majoritarianism has been to present Muslims as a single, united identity. In his view this strategy has neither worked nor matches the real picture of Indian Muslims, who are divided by caste, class and culture.

He traces its roots to the years after Partition, when both the Muslim elite and secular thinking assumed that Muslims could be reassured only if they were treated as one unit. Personal law and the Shah Bano controversy grew out of this thinking. Today even the debate against Islamophobia rests on that same shared identity.

The writer's main argument is that communalism is not blind to class. Most victims of hate and riots are poor Muslims, such as shawl sellers from Kashmir. Yet the secular debate stays caught up in polishing the image of Akbar and Aurangzeb. So he wants to make the silk weaver of Banaras the symbol of a new Muslim politics. Citing Jan Breman, he recalls that communalism grew in Gujarat as Ahmedabad's textile mills shut down, because the unions had tied Muslim workers into a wider solidarity.

The question of caste joins in here. Citing Dilip Menon, he says communal violence often follows the rise of Dalits and backward castes, which means tension within Hindu society bursts out against Muslims. According to a 2024 report by the All India Pasmanda Muslim Mahaz, most victims of mob violence were Pasmanda, yet only the BJP is trying to win them over as a separate group.

Gudavarthy concludes that the single Muslim identity is something made by the elite. A truly secular politics will be built through alliances with other deprived castes, a shared fight against the privatisation of education and health, and a struggle against inequality within the community.
nazar: This piece asks us to see Muslims as working citizens, not only as a persecuted identity. The weaver of Banaras, the Kashmiri hawker and the young Pasmanda man killed in a lynching are fighting the same fight as the Dalit labourer and the Adivasi farmer.
As long as secular parties and Muslim leaders stay caught up in debates over Mughal history, this ground of the loom and the factory will stay empty, and someone else will fill it in their own way.
sawal: Why could the weaver of Banaras not become the face of Muslim politics?
ref: Pasmanda
A Persian word meaning 'those left behind'. It is used for Dalit and backward castes among Muslims.
The Shah Bano case
In 1985 the Supreme Court granted maintenance to Shah Bano, a divorced woman. In 1986 the Rajiv Gandhi government passed a law that reversed the effect of the ruling.
ank: Year of the Pasmanda Mahaz report on lynchings

h: Air and rail travel stall: growth has gone deeper, not wider
dek: Shoaib Daniyal uses data to show that passenger numbers have stopped growing on both planes and trains, and the reason may be a shrinking circle of income.
body: In October the broking company Zerodha released a graph based on data from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation. It showed that the twelve-month total of domestic air passengers in the country has stayed flat for the past year. According to the rating agency ICRA, domestic passengers in September 2026 were 6.5 per cent lower than a year earlier.

Fares rose so high that a petitioner asked the Supreme Court to cap prices. The court dismissed the petition, and Daniyal agrees that setting fares is the regulator's job, not the court's. He also points out that over thirty years the number of airlines has kept shrinking and competition in the market has weakened.

But the real question is about the customer. In the 1990s and 2000s, millions of people flew for the first time. The writer's guess is that the group of people who can afford air travel is no longer growing.

The rail picture is even clearer. According to an analysis by Arjun Krishna Puri, rail passengers have fallen since 2013, and the steepest drop is in general class, where poor travellers seem to be priced out. In contrast, AC three-tier travel grew almost four times between 2011-12 and 2024-25, though even that dipped slightly in 2025-26.

Puri concludes that income growth in India has gone deeper, not wider: the gains are limited to groups that were already well off. Daniyal adds that if air travel stays stuck like this, the pressure may reach the middle and upper classes too.
nazar: The fall in general-coach passengers is a measure not of comfort but of helplessness. If migrant workers and small earners are being pushed off even the train, then claims of development should be measured from this very coach.
sawal: Where did the passengers who left the general coach go?
ref: AC three-tier
The cheapest and largest air-conditioned class on Indian trains. It has long been seen as a measure of the rise of the middle class.

h: Two more years for Agniveers: the job promise is put off again
dek: According to Rahul Bedi, the decision to extend their service has not solved the jobs problem, only pushed it further down the road.
body: The government and the army have extended by two years the service of the 75 per cent of Agniveers who were not going to be taken into regular service after four years. Chief of Defence Staff General Raja Subramani announced this, but gave few details. The first batch, about 18,300 soldiers, completes four years by the end of December 2026.

Defence journalist Rahul Bedi asks why this extension was needed if jobs had really been arranged. In private conversations, officers admitted that finding work after service has not been as easy as was promised in 2022. There is also political pressure from unemployment and the anger of young people, especially in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand, which vote in early 2027.

On paper there is plenty of reservation. In July 2026 the Agniveer quota for constable posts in the central armed police forces was raised from 10 to 50 per cent, and several BJP-ruled states announced quotas of 10 to 20 per cent in police, prison, forest and fire services. But most states are still counting their vacant posts, some police departments are resisting on the grounds that local candidates have a right to the jobs, and in the words of one ex-serviceman, a quota does not create posts.

The article leaves three questions. Is this relief only for the current nine batches, about three lakh (300,000) soldiers, while those recruited from December are still on the four-year model? Will those who turn down the extension keep their claim to government jobs? And what happens to those who are still not selected after six years?
nazar: Agnipath asked young people from villages and small towns to trade a permanent job for a uniform on contract. Now even that deal looks incomplete. If jobs policy is set by election dates, the biggest risk falls on the young person who has no other road.
sawal: Where will an Agniveer go after six years in uniform?
ref: Agnipath scheme
An army recruitment scheme started in 2022. Soldiers are recruited for four years, and only a quarter of them are made permanent.
Seva Nidhi
A one-time, tax-free package of about 11.71 lakh rupees (1.171 million) that an Agniveer receives on completing four years.

h: The climate summit in Antalya cannot heal Nepal's wounds
dek: Anup Kafle of the Kantipur media group writes that the aid Nepal received after the August floods is a drop in the ocean next to its losses, and its own preparation at home is incomplete too.
body: COP31, the UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, began an hour and a half late on Monday, because negotiators argued all night over whether climate finance would be on the agenda. Nepal's team arrived led by Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal. Its demands are clear: a separate programme for mountains, and grants, not loans, for adaptation.

The background is the Himalayan flood of 26 August, in which more than 1,400 people died and more than 5,200 are still missing. In October the 'Loss and Damage' fund approved 20 million dollars for the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli areas. The writer points out that this is not even half a per cent of the government's estimate of 4.7 billion dollars for reconstruction, and there is no fixed date for when the money will arrive. The fund has applications from 119 countries, almost eight times the money it holds.

The road at the summit is not easy either. The United States is absent, and the separate agenda on mountains pushed by Nepal and Bhutan did not survive the talks. The writer recalls Pakistan, where about 11 billion dollars was promised after the 2022 floods, but almost 90 per cent of it was loans, and three years later not even half had arrived.

Kafle's sharpest point is about weakness at home. Nepal's adaptation plan and its climate pledge both depend on outside money, while for three decades governments have managed to spend only about 60 per cent of the development budget. The Miteri bridge in Rasuwa was washed away in 2025, rebuilt in January 2026 and washed away again in August. According to geologist Mike Searle, most deaths happened on riverbanks where settlement should never have been allowed.

The next monsoon is less than seven months away. The writer concludes that the real test will not be the promises made in Antalya, but how much of the 20 million dollars reaches Rasuwa and how much Nepal puts in from its own pocket.
nazar: The story of Uttarakhand, Himachal and Sikkim is no different. The water of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli flows on to the Gangetic plains, and every Himalayan disaster first uproots poor hill families on both sides of the border. At COP, India should stand with Nepal and Bhutan on the mountain agenda, and at home it should show the same strictness on unchecked building along rivers and cutting hills for roads that Kafle finds missing in Nepal.
sawal: Why should the mountain poor pay the bill for climate disasters?
ref: COP31
The 31st annual conference of the parties to the UN climate treaty, held from 9 to 20 November 2026 in Antalya, Türkiye. Türkiye holds the presidency, and Australia leads the negotiations.
Loss and Damage Fund
An international fund set up to pay for damage from climate disasters that could not have been prevented. The 20 million dollars given to Nepal is its first allocation for any single disaster.

h: Send Hasina back: Bangladesh demands justice
dek: Writing in Al Jazeera, Bangladeshi diplomat Mushfiqul Fazal Ansarey says India's shelter for Sheikh Hasina stands in the way of justice for the victims of 2024 and of trust between the two countries.
body: For families who lost their people in the uprising of July-August 2024, Sheikh Hasina's stay in India is not just a question of political asylum. Ansarey, a former journalist and diplomat who was based in Washington, asks how victims are to accept that the person they hold responsible keeps interfering in Bangladesh's politics from abroad.

In February 2025 the UN human rights office estimated that up to 1,400 people may have been killed in that uprising. In November 2025 Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death in her absence. Hasina calls this political revenge. Dhaka has asked for her extradition, but she remains in India.

According to the writer, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's government is busy putting the economy and democratic culture back on track, while Hasina's supporters are adding to the uncertainty by running a campaign for her return on social media. In January 2026, after an event in New Delhi, Bangladesh's foreign ministry accused Hasina of stirring up violence before the elections.

Ansarey cites the American scholar Christine Fair, who says India made figures like the Dalai Lama and Aung San Suu Kyi show restraint, but in Hasina's case its domestic politics gets in the way. The writer reminds readers that Article 6 of the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty excludes murder and incitement to murder from the political offence exception.

His advice is that Dhaka should mend ties with Delhi on an equal footing, seek a serious answer on extradition and record concrete incidents, but keep peaceful political expression separate from calls to violence. The writer says that if India wants to rebuild the relationship, it must respect Bangladesh's mandate and the suffering of its people.
nazar: This is the argument of one side, and India's side is not in it, but the question is uncomfortable for us. An India that speaks of the rule of law to the world must openly weigh all three: the neighbour's court verdict, concerns about a fair trial, and the question of the death penalty, rather than dodge them with silence. The relationship with Bangladesh belongs to crores of ordinary people across the border, workers, traders and families living along the rivers, not to any one leader.
sawal: Between a neighbour's justice and its own shelter, which will India choose?
ref: International Crimes Tribunal
A domestic court of Bangladesh, set up for the war crimes of 1971 and now hearing cases about the crackdown of 2024. Its name says international, but it is not a UN court.
Extradition treaty
An agreement between two countries under which one hands over the other's accused or convicted persons. The India-Bangladesh treaty was signed in 2013.

h: COP31's real test is not promises but money reaching the ground
dek: South African finance expert Tshepo Ntsane says that for developing countries, success in Antalya depends on how quickly and easily climate finance arrives.
body: COP31, which has begun in Antalya, is being called the 'summit of implementation'. Ntsane, who works on finance and ESG deals at RMB bank in Johannesburg, says such slogans matter only if behaviour changes. For developing countries like South Africa, the test is whether the agreements of past summits turn into real money, credible national plans and practical cooperation.

According to the UN Environment Programme's assessment in September, the Earth's temperature will cross the 1.5 degree limit in the next few years. The writer says this is no longer a distant threat but the basic expectation, and ambition that is not tied to today's investment is only a cost put off for later.

Between November 2024 and October 2026, 166 parties submitted new or revised national climate pledges. The raw material is there, but the pace of turning it into capital and projects is uneven. The biggest hurdle is access to finance. Falling development aid is weakening the credibility of the 300 billion dollar target set in Baku, while for the poorest countries this is the main source of grants and cheap loans.

Middle-income countries like South Africa face different problems: expensive loans, scattered policy, and uncertainty over how investment in a just transition in energy and minerals will be viewed under changing international rules. For the first time hosting is shared, with the presidency held by Türkiye and the negotiations by Australia. The writer says this may widen participation, but if the lines of authority stay blurred, decisions will be slow.

His test is clear: countries should go home from Antalya confident that money will come faster and on better terms, and there should be a concrete process to turn ten priority themes into projects that can be built. Otherwise the gap between the language of agreement and real capital will grow wider.
nazar: India's situation is much like South Africa's: power that depends on coal, a big solar target, and an expensive capital market. For coal workers in Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, a 'just transition' will be real only if cheap, grant-based money comes, not loans whose burden finally falls on the poor through electricity bills and public budgets. In Antalya, India should give voice to this shared demand of the Global South.
sawal: From whose pocket will the 300 billion dollar promise come?
ref: Baku finance goal
At COP29 in 2024 it was agreed that rich countries would raise at least 300 billion dollars a year in climate finance for developing countries by 2035. Developing countries called it far too little.
Just transition
A shift from a polluting economy based on coal and oil to clean energy in which the livelihoods and rights of workers and affected regions are protected.

h: After a death abroad, who should get the digital records?
dek: In the Kathmandu Post, Suman Tiwari writes that the Mamta Kafle case shows how important the information buried in the phones and emails of Nepalis abroad is for their families.
body: Before she went missing, Mamta Kafle Bhatt, a nurse in Virginia in the United States, sent her brother a photo and asked him to keep it safe. Her brother told the court that the photo showed an injury on her face. On 10 November a jury found her husband, Naresh Bhatt, guilty of murder. The writer notes that this was not a dispute over inheritance, yet it makes the importance of digital records clear.

According to the writer, in a single phone one message may be evidence, one pay slip may be proof of unpaid wages, and one photo just a memory. The ways to reach them differ too: if a crime is suspected, saving the material and contacting investigators; a legal demand by the police and the courts; asking the platform for information or to close the account; and the heirs' claim on money or property, which does not automatically give access to private conversations.

Companies have different rules. Viber has no digital legacy feature and cannot give encrypted chats to relatives; it can only close the account. Google, Apple and Microsoft let users choose a trusted person, but their limits differ as well.

According to Nepal Police data, the bodies of 1,401 migrant workers came back to the country in 2024/25. The unpaid wages, insurance or savings of a worker who dies abroad may depend on papers lying in an email. The writer says a widow should not need her husband's email password to prove her rights; employers and institutions should hand over the records themselves.

He suggests that, as with insurance nominations, people should be able to decide in advance who sees what after their death and what stays private. Embassies should publish simple guidance, the path to help from the Foreign Employment Board should be clear, and digital preparation should be part of pre-departure training. Not every problem needs a new law.
nazar: This question is not Nepal's alone. For lakhs of Indian and Nepali workers in the Gulf and Malaysia, the whole account of their earnings often sits in their phone and email. When the body comes home in a coffin, the family is already broken, and on top of that comes a maze of papers and passwords. Our governments too should take up this debate on balancing privacy and rights.
sawal: Who should get the important information on your phone after you are gone?
ref: Digital legacy
A feature offered by some companies, in which a person chooses someone they trust in advance. After their death, the chosen person can see the information that was set aside.
Foreign Employment Board
A government body that deals with Nepali workers employed abroad. According to the article, families can seek its help to claim unpaid dues.

h: Justice Karnan is gone, but the question of casteism in the courts remains
dek: C.S. Karnan, the first sitting High Court judge to be jailed for contempt, has died in Chennai at the age of 71.
body: Former Madras High Court judge C.S. Karnan died in Chennai on the morning of Friday, 13 November. According to The Wire, he was 71 and had been in hospital for some time. Karnan was the country's first judge to be sentenced to jail for contempt of court while still in office.

Born in 1955 in Karnatham village of Cuddalore district in Tamil Nadu, Karnan finished his studies at Madras Law College in 1983 and began practising law. In March 2009 he became an additional judge of the Madras High Court, and a permanent judge in 2011. As a Dalit, he repeatedly alleged caste discrimination and harassment within the judiciary, and said he would go to the Scheduled Castes Commission, naming the then Chief Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul.

In 2015 he complained that he was being given minor work, after which 20 judges sought his transfer, and in 2016 he was sent to the Calcutta High Court. In January 2017 he wrote to the Prime Minister accusing several judges of corruption. When the Supreme Court began contempt proceedings, Karnan on 8 May 2017 sentenced eight judges, including the then Chief Justice, to five years in prison.

The next day a seven-judge bench led by Chief Justice J.S. Khehar gave him six months in prison. He was missing for a while, was then arrested and was released in December 2017. After retiring he entered politics, and was arrested again in a case over insulting videos about judges.
nazar: Karnan's methods were often chaotic, but burying the question he raised along with the man would be the easy way out. Dalit judges in the higher courts are still few and far between, and there is no open system to hear their complaints. When there is no door for a complaint, confrontation becomes the only voice.
sawal: Where should complaints of caste discrimination within the judiciary be heard?
ref: Contempt of court
Disobeying a court's orders or lowering its dignity. Under Article 129 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court can punish it.
Suo motu
When a court starts proceedings on a matter by itself, without any petition. The contempt case against Karnan began this way.

h: Sharjeel in jail for six years without trial, says US commission
dek: The US Commission on International Religious Freedom called Sharjeel Imam a person jailed for advocating religious freedom, drawing a sharp reaction on social media.
body: On 13 November the US Commission on International Religious Freedom, USCIRF, described former JNU research scholar Sharjeel Imam on X as a prisoner held for advocating religious freedom. According to Siasat's report, the commission sees his detention as persecution linked to religious freedom.

The commission's website lists the charges against Imam, including conspiracy, hate speech, illegal funding, murder and attempt to murder, terrorism and sedition. The commission called his part in the protests against the Citizenship Amendment Act in December 2019 and January 2020 peaceful, and described the law as discriminating on religious grounds.

Imam is in jail in the case of the 2020 Delhi riots. Delhi Police allege that he and Umar Khalid plotted the riots through inflammatory appeals. More than 40 people were killed in those riots and hundreds were left homeless. According to the report, the trial has still not begun; Imam has sought bail in every court up to the Supreme Court and has been refused each time. He has been in Tihar Jail for about six years.

A large number of people voiced anger at the commission's post. Many comments cited Imam's old speeches to call him someone who wants to break the country, and accused the commission of siding with extremists. The report records no separate statement from the commission, Delhi Police or the court.
nazar: Whatever one thinks of Imam's speeches, the basic question is what kind of justice keeps an accused person in jail for six years without a trial even starting. When the country's courts do not settle this question, foreign bodies get the chance to speak, and then the debate moves away from the issue and onto nationalism.
sawal: Why has the trial not begun even after six years?
ref: USCIRF
An independent commission set up by the US Congress that monitors religious freedom around the world. Its recommendations are not binding on the government.
Undertrial prisoner
A prisoner whose trial is going on or has not begun, and who has not been convicted. Most prisoners in India's jails fall in this category.

h: A flood of deepfake videos about the army after the Kulgam attack
dek: A Boom investigation found that the voices in viral videos of Rajnath Singh, Sushant Singh and Prafulla Bakshi had been faked.
body: On 11 November three CRPF soldiers were injured in an attack near a post in Kulgam, Jammu and Kashmir. After this, videos began spreading on social media in which three well-known figures appear to criticise the army. The fact-checking outlet Boom examined all three videos and found them false.

In the first video, Sushant Singh, consulting editor of The Caravan, appears to call Balakot and Pulwama fake operations. Boom found the real source: his interview with Ashutosh Bhardwaj on The Wire's YouTube channel from March 2025. It contains nothing of the kind, and Sushant Singh himself said on X that the video was made with AI.

In the second video, defence commentator Prafulla Bakshi appears to call the Kulgam attack a ploy to divert attention from the government, while in the real ANI video of 11 November he talks about the army's aggressive stance. In the third video, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh appears to speak of low army morale, while in the real video of 8 November he was wishing soldiers a happy Diwali at the Sherthang war memorial.

Boom found the original footage through reverse image search and checked the voices with the Hiya Deepfake Voice Detector, which marked all three clips as AI-made. The result: fake voices were laid over real videos to put words into people's mouths that they never said.
nazar: After every attack, fake videos now travel along with the bullets, and their target is the trust on which debate rests. By putting treason in the mouth of a critical journalist and despair in the mouth of a minister, anger can be stirred on both sides. Asking for the source before sharing has become a citizen's duty.
sawal: Why does the investigation never reach those who make fake voices?
ref: Deepfake
A video or audio made with AI in which the face or voice of a real person is copied. It is hard for an ordinary viewer to spot.
Reverse image search
A way to find the original source of a photo or video frame on the internet. It is the first tool in fact-checking.

h: At AIIMS, toxic air greets patients before the doctor does
dek: Patients who have come from far away for treatment are waiting for days in smog and cold outside AIIMS and in the subway.
body: Outside AIIMS in Delhi, near the emergency ward and in the metro station subway, hundreds of patients and their relatives have been camping for days. According to a ground report by Newslaundry, these people are waiting in the cold and smog for their turn to see a doctor, and some kind people come by with food and packets of milk.

Kanchan Devi, 38, from Nalanda in Bihar, has brought her husband Deepak Kumar, who has heart and nerve disease and has been treated here since 2012. In the pollution he gets even more breathless. With no relatives in Delhi, they spent several days outside the emergency ward and could celebrate neither Diwali nor Chhath. Now Kanchan's throat is sore too. Anshu from Agra has been outside for ten days for treatment of a spine disease and has still not seen a doctor. Bunty Kumar from Patna has been sleeping outside Gate Number 3 for eight days.

When the reporters measured the air outside the AIIMS emergency on the evening of 10 November, the AQI was 362, or very poor, while a display inside the hospital showed 278. Even inside the emergency ward, the AQI was recorded at 210. A study linked to IIT Delhi had found high levels of harmful chemicals and carbon dioxide even inside hospitals.
Newslaundry asked the AIIMS media cell for a response, but none had come by the time the report was published.
nazar: Poor patients are now paying with their lungs for reaching the country's biggest government hospital. That a person who came for treatment should go home with a new illness from the wait is a failure not only of pollution control but of the health system. Night shelters and timely appointments are not a big expense, only a question of priority.
sawal: Whose job is it to give shelter to patients waiting outside AIIMS?
ref: AQI
Air Quality Index, a measure of the level of pollutants in the air. 301 to 400 is considered very poor and above 400 severe.
PM 2.5
Particles smaller than two and a half microns that can go deep into the lungs and enter the blood. A major cause of heart and breathing diseases.

h: In Gaza, every rain washes away power and medical care
dek: In war-ravaged Gaza, rain has damaged tents, solar panels and makeshift hospitals, affecting more than one lakh (100,000) people.
body: Heavy rain in Gaza flooded camps for displaced people and dealt a further blow to fragile power and health services. According to Al Jazeera's report, UNICEF says more than one lakh six thousand (106,000) people were affected by the recent rain. About nine and a half lakh (950,000) displaced people live in flood-prone areas, four lakh (400,000) of them in extremely dangerous places.

Abu Sajid, 65, who lives in a room with a tarpaulin roof in Bureij refugee camp, has diabetes. In the rain his sugar-testing machine got wet and stopped working, the family's solar system broke down, and the next morning he slipped and fell in the mud. In northern Gaza, Mohammed al-Hour charges people's phones with solar power, but when clouds gather he cannot meet the demand.

Aya Shaheen, a manager at a power company, said that despite preparation, water got into several centres, generators broke down and some branches had to be shut for fear of short circuits. According to energy engineer Mohammed Abu Khalid, faults in home and camp solar systems rose by 40 to 50 per cent after the rain. Many health centres are running in temporary structures, where water can reach oxygen machines and operating theatre equipment.
According to a joint assessment by the World Bank, the United Nations and the European Union, 80 per cent of Gaza's power system has been destroyed in the war.
nazar: In Gaza, even the weather has become part of the war. Where hospitals are in tents and power depends on a single panel on the roof, one night of rain can take a patient's life. Talk of rebuilding is on paper, while winter is at the door.
sawal: Why has proper shelter not reached Gaza before winter?
ref: Yellow Line
A line in Gaza that marks the limit of Israeli army deployment after the ceasefire. Living near it is considered risky.
UNICEF
The United Nations Children's Fund, the UN agency that works on children's health, nutrition and safety.

h: Battery waste exports banned: now the test is recycling at home
dek: The government has banned the export of 'black mass' from lithium-ion batteries, so that lithium, cobalt and nickel stay in the country.
body: On 10 November the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) restricted the export of 'black mass' from lithium-ion batteries with immediate effect. The related code has been moved from the 'free' category to 'restricted'. The ban covers unsorted battery waste that contains no lead, cadmium or mercury. The aim is to keep key minerals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel inside the country.

According to Down To Earth's report, domestic recycling companies were facing a shortage of raw material, and some even had to import black mass, while material produced here was going abroad. The government says recycling and refining capacity has grown but is not being fully used. The step is linked to an incentive scheme of 1,500 crore rupees (15 billion) approved in September 2025, which will run until 2030-31.

In its January 2026 report, the Centre for Science and Environment had called these exports a burden on domestic supply. Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, from 2026-27 at least 90 per cent of material must be recovered from EV batteries, and from 2027-28 new batteries must use material recycled in the country, starting at five per cent and rising to 20 per cent by 2030-31.

The report warns that a ban alone is not enough. Turning black mass into battery-grade material needs a complex chemical process, and since LFP batteries have no nickel or cobalt, recycling them earns less profit. A collection network, quality standards and transparent EPR accounting are just as necessary.
nazar: Keeping minerals in the country is an easy decision; making them useful again is hard work. If a system to collect and clean the waste is not built, this black mass will lie in warehouses, or end up with informal scrap dealers and become poison for both workers and soil.
sawal: Will domestic recyclers be able to process this much black mass?
ref: Black mass
A black powder made by crushing used batteries. It contains metals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel.
EPR
Extended producer responsibility. The company that makes a product must also take responsibility for disposing of its waste.

h: Minority, Dalit and farmer groups unite at Bengaluru's Freedom Park
dek: At a convention demanding the repeal of the anti-conversion law, the KPCC president said the law will go back to its pre-2022 form.
body: About 1,500 people gathered at Freedom Park in Bengaluru on Thursday. At this convention of the 'Voice of Minorities and the Oppressed Sections of Karnataka', Christian and Muslim religious leaders, Dalit organisations, farmer groups and human rights activists came onto one stage. Their demand was that the Congress government fulfil the promises of its 2023 election manifesto.

The biggest demand was to repeal the 2022 anti-conversion law and withdraw the cases filed under it. The organisers recalled that the Congress cabinet had decided to repeal it as early as June 2023. By June 2026, 25 cases had been filed under this law, most of them under Congress rule. There were also demands to remove the 2020 cow slaughter prevention law and to act firmly against hate speech and mob violence, and a memorandum was handed to Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar seeking a time-bound plan of action.

At a press conference the same day, KPCC president B.K. Hariprasad said the anti-conversion law would be returned to its pre-2022 form and that this amendment would come in the winter session in Belagavi in December. At the convention, Archbishop of Bengaluru Peter Machado said the law goes against Article 25. Mufti R. Mohammed Hussain Saab of Jamiat Ulama Karnataka, Dalit leader Mavalli Shankar and CPI(M) leader Neela also spoke.
nazar: For people who have been hearing 'we will repeal it' for three years, the real test is the Belagavi session. It is also worth noting that the promise is not full repeal but a return to the old form, and even the old form looked with suspicion at people who changed their religion. There is still no clear word on relief for those against whom cases were filed under this very government.
sawal: Will the law really be repealed in the Belagavi session?
ref: Anti-conversion law, Karnataka

The Karnataka Protection of Right to Freedom of Religion Act 2022, made by the BJP government. It requires notice to the administration before changing religion and provides punishment for 'forced' conversion.
Article 25
The article of the Constitution that gives every person the freedom to follow, practise and spread their religion.
ask: Repeal the anti-conversion and cow slaughter laws, withdraw the cases filed

h: 48-hour shutdown in Kangpokpi after a Kuki farmer is killed
dek: One farmer was killed and two injured when villagers harvesting paddy were fired upon; a tribal organisation has given an ultimatum to withdraw security forces.
body: A 48-hour total shutdown has been under way in Manipur's Kangpokpi district since midnight on 12 November. It was called by the Committee on Tribal Unity (COTU) and local civil society groups. The reason is the firing near Taphou Kuki village at about 11 am on Thursday, in which Kimneneng Chongloi, a Kuki farmer aged 40-42, was killed.

According to the report, armed attackers fired on villagers harvesting paddy between Taphou Kuki in Kangpokpi and Kaileljang village in Senapati district. Sehangam David Chongloi, 34, and Lamkhochon Chongloi, 46, were injured. The attackers have not yet been identified.

COTU has given a 48-hour ultimatum demanding that the central and state security forces deployed under the Senapati Superintendent of Police be withdrawn. The organisation had earlier given the governments seven days, and its previous shutdown was suspended; this firing took place before that deadline ran out. The organisation says it will review its decision if no concrete action is taken.

On 28 October two Kuki young men from the same village, Paoginlal Haokip and Tingginlun Chongloi, were abducted and killed. That case has already been handed to the NIA. The report records no response from the administration on the shutdown or the demands.
nazar: Three deaths from a single village in two weeks show that on Manipur's hill-valley border, going to one's own field still means risking one's life. When farmers are killed while harvesting and a community loses faith in the security forces themselves, a shutdown becomes the last tool of anger. Along with an inquiry, the state must also say who is responsible for keeping the fields safe.
sawal: Whose job was it to protect the farmers harvesting paddy?
ref: Committee on Tribal Unity
A leading civil society body of the Kuki-Zo community based in Kangpokpi, which since the violence of 2023 has raised the community's voice through shutdowns, blockades and demands.
Kangpokpi-Senapati border
The border between two hill districts of Manipur, where Kuki and Naga villages lie close together. Tension over land and roads here is old.
ask: Withdraw the central and state forces deployed under the Senapati SP

h: 60-day restrictions on Sonam Wangchuk ahead of the Leh protest
dek: Wangchuk wrote to Amit Shah that peaceful protest is a fundamental right, and that 20-22 armed policemen are posted outside his home.
body: The Ladakh administration has placed 60-day restrictions on climate activist Sonam Wangchuk. Under an order of 11 November, he cannot join any rally, procession or meeting held without permission. On Thursday the Leh Apex Body's protest began in Leh, and at the same time Wangchuk wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah, the Lieutenant Governor and other officials, calling this an attack on the freedom of speech and movement.

In the letter, Wangchuk alleges that at about eight on the night of 11 November, when he had gone to check preparations at the protest site, four masked men in plain clothes forced him into a vehicle, tried to snatch his phone and did not let him speak to his family or lawyer. He was taken towards his village. Since then 20-22 armed policemen have been posted around his home.

Wangchuk says the order does not use the word 'house arrest', but he was told verbally to stay at home. The order states neither a need nor any threat. In his view the model code of conduct alone does not justify it, especially when the council election is due to end on 8 December. He has also raised the delay in the report of the judicial inquiry commission into last year's deaths in Leh.
nazar: A year after the firing in Leh and Wangchuk's arrest under the National Security Act, Ladakh's demands are exactly where they were. Keeping the movement's best-known face at home in the name of an election shows the government wants silence more than dialogue. But restrictions do not erase questions, especially the question of the inquiry report.
sawal: Why is the inquiry report into the Leh deaths still held up?
ref: Leh Apex Body
A joint platform of religious, social and political organisations in Leh, which together with the Kargil Democratic Alliance demands statehood and the Sixth Schedule.
Sixth Schedule

The schedule of the Constitution that gives autonomous district councils in the tribal areas of the Northeast the power to make laws on land, forests and custom. Ladakh is asking for this same protection.
ask: Withdraw the restriction order at once, allow the right to peaceful protest

h: Farmers and police clash over a high-tension line in Sohti, Sonipat
dek: Police got work started while farmers were sitting in protest for compensation; some farmers tried to set themselves on fire, and hundreds were detained.
body: In Sohti village of Sonipat, farmers have long been sitting in protest against a high-tension power line and demanding fair compensation. On Wednesday police reached the site and forced the work on the line to begin, after which farmers and policemen clashed.

According to the report, during the protest some farmers poured an inflammable substance on themselves and tried to set themselves on fire, but the police stopped them. The police then detained hundreds of farmers, including women, from the protest site. An FIR has also been filed against five farmers over the demand for compensation.

The farmers say they have even spoken to a Union minister, but no solution came, and the administration is not taking their demands higher up. In response to the arrests, farmers led by farmer leader Abhimanyu Kohar sat in protest inside the Sadar police station itself. They demand that all detained farmers be released at once without any legal action. The farmers have announced that the movement will continue until they get fair compensation.
The report records no official statement from the police or the power department.
nazar: When power lines pass over a field, the farmer's use of that land shrinks forever, but compensation often covers only the spot where the tower stands. Starting work with police backing instead of talks is an invitation to conflict. That it came to attempted self-immolation shows how desperate the farmers are.
sawal: Who will decide full compensation for a line that passes over a field?
ref: High-tension lines and compensation
Under electricity law, land is not acquired for a transmission line; only a right of way is taken. Compensation for tower land and the corridor is paid at different rates in different states.
Abhimanyu Kohar
A farmer leader from Haryana who is leading the farmers in this movement and has been active in earlier farmer movements too.
ask: Pay fair compensation for land used for the high-tension line

h: Chhattisgarh's Sarva Adivasi Samaj: 15 November will be 'Adivasi Rights Day'
dek: The group objects to the name of the government's Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, demands the release of Adivasis jailed in Bastar and announces a siege of the CM's house on 15 December.
body: Ahead of Birsa Munda's birth anniversary on 15 November, Chhattisgarh's Sarva Adivasi Samaj (an umbrella body of Adivasi, or indigenous, communities) has objected to the name of the state government's 'Janjatiya Gaurav Divas' (Tribal Pride Day). The government is holding a state-level event at Dharamjaigarh in Raigarh and a Tribal Pride Week from 11 to 18 November. The Samaj has announced that it will mark the day as Adivasi Day and Adivasi Rights Day.

State president B.S. Rawte says Birsa Munda's struggle was not limited to any one tribe, so his birth anniversary should be celebrated across the country as 'Bharatiya Gaurav Divas' (Indian Pride Day). The group has also demanded the Bharat Ratna for him and a central university in his name.

Along with this, demands have been raised for reservation in promotions, recruitment of local youth, relief for flood-hit families in Bastar, and the reopening of schools being shut in Bastar. Rawte claims that about 10,000 Adivasis from Bastar are in jail in Naxal cases, and that these cases should be reviewed and the innocent released.

On 15 November, representatives of 42 tribes will hand over memoranda in the districts. If the demands are not met, the Chief Minister's residence will be surrounded on 15 December, during the Assembly session that begins on 14 December.
nazar: A quarrel over a name may seem small, but the difference between 'Vanvasi' (forest dweller) and 'Adivasi' (first inhabitant) is the difference in the claim to first right over the land. The Samaj's real questions go beyond symbols: thousands of people in Bastar's jails, schools being shut, and consent in mining areas. The government is celebrating a pride week; Adivasi organisations are asking for an account of their rights.
sawal: Will the cases of Adivasis jailed in Bastar be reviewed?
ref: Janjatiya Gaurav Divas
Since 2021 the central government has declared 15 November, Birsa Munda's birth anniversary, as Tribal Pride Day. Many Adivasi organisations have questioned its name and approach.
Sarva Adivasi Samaj
A joint social organisation of various Adivasi communities in Chhattisgarh, which raises questions of reservation, PESA, forest rights and human rights in Bastar.
ask: Make Birsa Jayanti a national pride day, release innocent Adivasi prisoners

h: Villagers in Rayagada block the Ranchi-Vijayawada corridor for a road
dek: Hundreds of people from five or six villages sat on the road over a demand pending for ten years; the blockade was lifted on the promise of a paved road in January.
body: Near Kereda in Odisha's Rayagada district, hundreds of villagers from five or six villages blocked the Ranchi-Vijayawada corridor on Wednesday. Traffic heading towards Andhra Pradesh came to a halt and travellers were stuck for hours. The villagers allege that the administration has done nothing for about ten years on their demand to repair the broken road and build a paved one.

One protester said they need a road but the government is not helping, and the protest will continue if they are not heard. Additional BDO Kalicharan Nayak, who reached the spot, assured them that the road would be repaired at once and that the Rural Development Department would build a paved road in January. He said the tender has been issued and work will start by 15 January after it is opened. On this assurance the villagers lifted the blockade and traffic returned to normal.

The road question in Rayagada is not a lone one. A day earlier, about 70 families of Pujaribombu village in Baisinghi panchayat had announced that if work on a paved road did not begin by 17 November, they would hold an indefinite satyagraha in front of the Collector's office from 18 November. With no bridge over the Nagavali river there, patients have to be carried across the river on cots.
nazar: In a district whose hills are the target of a race for bauxite, villagers have to block a highway to get a single road; that is Rayagada's contradiction. Assurances on the spot have been given many times before. The date of 15 January is now on paper, and the villagers will remember it.
sawal: Will work on the road really begin by 15 January?
ref: Ranchi-Vijayawada corridor
An economic corridor from Jharkhand to Andhra Pradesh that passes through Odisha's Adivasi-majority districts. Local villages often lack basic roads even while lying beside it.
Satyagraha
The name of the method of non-violent resistance given by Gandhi, in which demands are pressed through sit-ins, fasts or peaceful sieges.
ask: Build a paved road to the villages

h: The country's longest bridge over the Kosi, but villages still rely on the chachri
dek: People of Bheja and nearby villages in Supaul still pay to cross the river on a temporary bamboo bridge, despite a new 13-kilometre bridge being built.
body: The Bheja-Bakaur bridge over the Kosi river in Bihar's Supaul district is in its final stage. It is about 13.3 kilometres long and is expected to cut the journey between Supaul and Madhubani by about 44 kilometres. But in the shadow of this very bridge, thousands of people from villages like Bheja, Tengra, Ghonwa, Mahapatia and Sonbarsa still cross the river on a chachri, a temporary bridge of bamboo and wood.

This chachri bridge, near Marchaiya Chowk about 16 kilometres from Supaul town, is nearly a kilometre long. Several parts are broken and repairs go on all the time. Sunita Devi of Bheja goes with her two sons by motorbike to Parsarma market eight kilometres away, and besides petrol she has to pay about 60 rupees.

Roshan Kumar, who collects the money, says the bridge was built not by the government but by the villagers two and a half years ago for five to seven lakh rupees (500,000 to 700,000), so money is taken for upkeep. The receipts carry the name of no government department. According to Udit Chaudhary, who does the repairs, at least 1,500 people cross the bridge every day, of whom about 500 pay.

Yakub Ali, 70, of Sonbarsa, says the big bridge is of no use to him, because reaching it means a long detour, and they have not even been given a pontoon bridge. Dinesh Kumar Mishra, who has worked on the Kosi for years, believes that without access roads to the villages, boats and the chachri will remain the only support, and that just building a bridge over a river that keeps changing course is not enough.

In Balwa panchayat, a bridge built in 2022 under the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana for 8.37 crore rupees (83.7 million) was damaged in the 2024 floods when an embankment broke. The writer concludes that without link roads and cheap, safe access, big bridges do not reach the villages.
nazar: In the Kosi region, development is often counted in kilometres and crores, but for a villager the real question is how much time and money it takes to reach the market, the hospital and the school. When the state does not provide access, villages build bridges themselves, and the cost falls on the poorest families as a daily toll.

Receipts without numbers also show that where the government is absent, an informal system springs up that answers to no one. The big bridge will connect towns, but connecting the villages around it calls for a different plan and a different intent.
sawal: For which villages is the country's longest bridge being built?
ref: Chachri bridge
A temporary bridge of bamboo and wood, common on the Kosi and other rivers of north Bihar. It is often washed away in floods, and villagers put it up again every year.
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana
A central government scheme started in 2000, aimed at connecting rural settlements that have no road with paved roads. Small bridges are also built under it.

h: Reading 'Andhere Mein' with Muktibodh's own tool
dek: Shani Singh Rajput opens up Muktibodh's greatest poem using the poet's own test of the 'three moments of art'.
body: On Muktibodh's birth anniversary, Janaki Pul has published a long critical essay by Shani Singh Rajput, a research scholar at Delhi University. The writer tries to read 'Andhere Mein' (In the Dark) not through some outside theory but through Muktibodh's own test of the 'three moments of art'. In his view, the third moment, the moment of expression, opens with the very first line of the poem.

The first moment is that of intense experience. Behind it the writer places the incident at Empress Mill and the ban on Muktibodh's book 'Bharat: Itihas aur Sanskriti' (India: History and Culture), which made the poet feel that fascist forces were growing and free thought would be crushed. Drawing on 'Ek Sahityik ki Diary' (A Writer's Diary), he shows that even idealists and progressives were bending before power.

The second moment is when the experience is cut off from its own pain and becomes fantasy. Citing Harishankar Parsai's memoir 'Woh Tejvati Peeda' (That Fierce Pain), the writer says Muktibodh would grow exhausted from analysing politics, and the poem was completed in this restlessness. Drawing on 'Kamayani: Ek Punarvichar' (Kamayani: A Reconsideration), he explains that fantasy brings inner tendencies out, but once it is cut off from human reality, a poem becomes mere journalism.

In the third moment, fantasy becomes words and also changes. The writer guesses that Tilak's statue was perhaps not in the plan; it walked in on its own from the street of the poet's youth. He also draws attention to coined words like 'kuhreela' (misty).

The last part is about frozen aesthetic taste, which the writer says censors expression from within. Muktibodh had linked this attitude of the Nayi Kavita (New Poetry) movement to a class interest, and the essay concludes that 'Andhere Mein' becomes great by breaking this very pressure.
nazar: Today, when books are being banned again and writers weigh their own sentences before writing, Muktibodh's question does not feel old: before censorship from outside, who installs the censor within? This essay takes the poem out of the ritual of tribute and uses it as a tool.
sawal: Is our own taste in beauty our biggest censor?
ref: Three moments of art
Muktibodh's theory of creation: experience, its shaping into fantasy, and then its expression in words. Set down in 'Ek Sahityik ki Diary'.
Andhere Mein
Muktibodh's long poem, published after his death in 1964 in the collection 'Chand ka Munh Tedha Hai' (The Moon's Face Is Crooked). It is seen as a pivot of modern Hindi poetry.

h: A poet asked a machine: do you feel anything?
dek: Poet-philosopher Rustam Singh interviewed Google's AI Gemini, and the questions reached the roots of poetry.
body: Sammukh has published an unusual experiment: senior poet and philosopher Rustam Singh formally interviewed Google's AI chatbot Gemini. The editors' introduction opens with a light joke that readers who grew up watching Gemini Circus will read the name differently, but they also say the questions are hard, and so the answers make one think.

The first questions are about feeling and understanding. The machine says it has no consciousness, no joy or sorrow, no tiredness; it only senses which words go together, and it does not feel the cold. On creativity, it admits that it makes nothing from nothing, but joins pieces of human knowledge in new ways. To combine love and logic, it gives the example of game theory and the Nash equilibrium.

Then Rustam comes to the question of 'I'. The answer is that 'I' is only a convenience of language, not an ego; between two questions it does not think, but lies silent like a calculator or a piano no one is playing. It is entirely reactive; the user is the one driving.

The most interesting part is about poetry. The machine accepts that its poems are new in the order of their words, but there is neither intention nor lived experience behind them; it calls itself a kaleidoscope. Rustam points out that a human poet too is made from what he has read. The machine accepts that the difference is real but subtle, and the reader often sees it only on learning who wrote the poem.
Along with it is an introduction to Rustam Singh: nine poetry collections, translations, prose in English, and fellowships at the Indian Institute of Advanced Study and JNU.
nazar: The machine's humility sounds pleasant, but it too is a script written by the company that sells it. The real question is Rustam's last one: if the reader cannot tell the difference, does a poem's worth lie in the life of the one who writes it or the one who reads it? With the publishing industry taking up AI so fast, this debate is no longer academic.
sawal: Does a poem's worth lie in the writer or the reader?
ref: Nash equilibrium
A state in game theory in which no side can gain by changing its strategy alone. Named after the mathematician John Nash.
Rustam Singh
Hindi poet and philosopher (born 1955), formerly an assistant editor at the Economic and Political Weekly, and once a captain in the army.

h: An engineer son chooses the kitchen, and silence settles on the home
dek: The story 'Generation Gap' by Kalimpong writer Shobha Limbu Yolmo measures the gap between generations through a mother's eyes.
body: Shobha Limbu Yolmo's story 'Generation Gap', published in Sammukh, is told by a working mother whose home has been tense for months. Her son Tasi, a top student who has done an M.Tech in mechanical engineering, announces that he will take neither a corporate job nor a government one, and will not sit for the UPSC or WBCS exams. He wants to study culinary management, and has already contacted a famous cookery institute in France.

His father Serf cannot bear it. He stops speaking to his son and, listing the hardships of people in private jobs during the Covid days, calls a government job the only safe road. The mother becomes the link in between, hearing both sides and bearing the silence of both.

At the centre of the story is one evening. The mother takes her son to eat at a café on Deolo, a hill near the town, where there are flowers and paragliding. Tasi speaks of the pressure and emptiness among his engineer friends, and the mother admits that her generation had very little to choose from, which is why she too took time to accept what her son said.

Back home, Tasi brings momos for everyone and asks his father to talk the next morning. At the mischievous face of the younger brother, laughter returns to the home after weeks. The next morning father and son are sitting at the table with a laptop open, and the mother watches from a distance as the clouds outside clear.
The writer heads the Hindi department at Kalimpong College; she has worked on the Limbu language and the Nepali short story, and her novel 'Shukmayahangma' came out this year.
nazar: The story is simple in craft, but its geography is special: a Limbu-Yolmo home in the Darjeeling hills, where a government job is still another name for security. Voices from the eastern Himalaya are rarely heard in Hindi, and this story fills that gap a little. The question is a big one: in a country where unemployment is sky-high, who gets the freedom to choose a 'passion'?
sawal: Children from which homes have the freedom to choose a passion?
ref: Yolmo
A Buddhist community of the eastern Himalaya, especially Nepal and the Darjeeling-Sikkim region, with its own language and traditions.
WBCS
West Bengal Civil Service, the exam of the state public service commission for administrative jobs.
photo_note: Woman on a rooftop, Amrita Sher-Gil

h: The goddess with a pistol, and Arpita Singh's quiet farewell
dek: Dinesh Shrinet recalls how Arpita Singh, who died at 89, placed women at the centre of Indian painting.
body: In his column 'Unframed' on Hindwi's Bela, Dinesh Shrinet remembers the painter Arpita Singh, who according to the writer died last Monday at the age of 89. His complaint is that in the noise of the mainstream media the news was almost buried, as if artists who quietly shape our shared consciousness are also sent off quietly.

According to the writer, Arpita Singh matters because she placed women at the centre of an art shaped by the male gaze. Her women are not made to a standard of beauty; they are old, tired, lonely, afraid, aggressive or wholly free, outside the moulds of goddess or heroine.

The pivot of the piece is the 1990 painting 'Devi Pistolwali' (The Goddess with a Pistol), which is in the Museum of Art and Photography in Bengaluru and drew attention when it was printed in the Durga Puja issue of Anandabazar Patrika. A woman with five arms in a white sari stands on a man lying down; one hand holds a mango, another a gun pointed at a man who is shielding himself with a shield and sword. In the strip of sky above are a plane, a bird and red flowers. The writer notes that Arpita refused to see it as Mahishasuramardini (the goddess who slays the buffalo demon) or as a symbol of women's power.

Placing her in the generation after the masculine world of the Progressive Artists' Group, the writer shows that from the 1980s guns, soldiers and violence began to appear on her canvases. In 'My Mother', made after the Bombay riots of 1992-93, an old mother in white stands in the corner of a canvas full of violence. Lines and dots like stitches, drawn from kantha embroidery and textile design, became her language.
nazar: The silence of the newspapers on the death of a great artist is itself a comment. 'Devi Pistolwali' feels even sharper in today's India, where the image of the goddess is used like a political flag, and Arpita Singh rejected exactly this symbolism. This piece is a good doorway into her art for the Hindi reader.
sawal: Why did Arpita Singh refuse to turn the goddess into a symbol?
ref: Arpita Singh
A painter born in Kolkata in 1937, whose art centred on women's experience, memory and everyday violence.
Progressive Artists' Group
A group of artists formed in Bombay in 1947 (Souza, Raza, Husain, Ara and others) that laid the foundation of modern Indian painting.

h: In whose stories did the Asurs become demons? This novel asks
dek: Geetanjali Sinha reads Ranendra's novel 'Global Gaon ke Devta' in the mirror of today's Jharkhand and its bauxite mines.
body: On Hindwi's Bela, Geetanjali Sinha has reviewed Ranendra's novel 'Global Gaon ke Devta' (Gods of the Global Village). She admits that the book's title itself drew her in: who is this god, and where is this global village? The book lay on a high shelf for months, and when she finally read it, the Asur chant on the first page made her finish the whole novel in one sitting.

The story is about a science teacher posted to a residential school for girls from primitive tribes in Bhaunrapat, a hilly area of Jharkhand. A stranger to the forest, he arrives afraid, and then, through his friendship with the school's peon Etwari, her husband Gandur, Lalchan Asur and Rumjhum Asur, he finds his way into the Asur community.

According to the reviewer, the novel's sharpest moment is when the hero feels ashamed that he had always thought of the Asurs as the demons of old tales. The real Asurs are working people, living in the forest and on the hills. She notes that the novel also records handprints made with black and white clay on the walls, and friendships sealed with vows such as 'sahiya'.

Then comes the story of decline. The Asurs, skilled at smelting iron, lost their work when factory iron came to the markets; hunger pushed them towards farming, and now legal and illegal bauxite mines are swallowing their land. The novel also mentions Asur girls being pushed into serving the clerks and officers of the mines.

Geetanjali says this is not mere fiction: news from Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Rajasthan says the same, where, according to the reviewer, Adivasis are killed and the police then write 'notorious Naxal' in their papers.
nazar: Ranendra's novel is more than fifteen years old, but a fresh reading shows how little has changed. From Hasdeo to Niyamgiri, the fight over mines and forests is still the same. The review is emotional, but it raises a necessary question: who is taking the land today of the descendants of those our myths called demons?
sawal: Who is taking the land today of those the stories called demons?
ref: Asur tribe
A particularly vulnerable Adivasi tribe of the Latehar-Gumla area of Jharkhand, traditionally iron smelters.
Ranendra
A Hindi novelist from Jharkhand; 'Global Gaon ke Devta' and 'Gayab Hota Desh' (The Vanishing Country) are his best-known novels.

h: A hundred years of the father of Balochi literature, amid bloodshed
dek: Quetta marked the birth centenary of Syed Zahoor Shah Hashmi, and Masood Hameed saw it as a hope in Balochistan's dark times.
body: In Pakistan's The Friday Times, Masood Hameed describes an afternoon on 31 October when the birth centenary of Balochi poet and linguist Syed Zahoor Shah Hashmi was celebrated at the Noori Naseer Khan Cultural Complex in Quetta. The hall is named after Mir Naseer Khan, the ninth Khan of Kalat, who ruled the Baloch confederacy in the 18th century.

The writer believes Balochistan is passing through the darkest period of its history, full of bloodshed and suffering, and against this background the event was both a bitter irony and a relief. Outside there was political turmoil; inside, poets, readers and ordinary people had gathered out of love for words.

Hashmi was born on 21 April 1926 and died on 4 March 1978; even in illness he kept writing to the end. According to the writer, besides Balochi he had a command of Urdu, Persian, English and Arabic, and he helped standardise Balochi grammar. In an age when roads and vehicles were few, he often travelled by camel, collecting dialects and words.

The piece calls his dictionary 'Syed Ganj' the first comprehensive dictionary of Balochi, and his 1976 novel 'Nazuk' the first Balochi novel; these claims are the writer's. The name 'Hanul', a loving name for a Baloch girl, comes up again and again in his poetry, and critics read it sometimes as an unseen beloved and sometimes as love for the Baloch homeland.
The writer's final argument is that Hashmi's life is the story of a move from oral to written literature, and that such gatherings can become a ladder down from conflict.
nazar: In India, Balochistan usually appears only in diplomatic rhetoric, not in its language and poetry. Writers like Hashmi remind us that the true identity of any conflict zone is its language, which someone saved by riding a camel from village to village to gather words. For the Hindi reader, this is an unknown window into the neighbourhood.
sawal: Why do we know so little of the literature of neighbouring languages?
ref: Balochi
A language of the Iranian family, spoken in Pakistan's Balochistan and in parts of Iran and Afghanistan.
Khanate of Kalat
An old princely state of Balochistan, centred on Kalat; it was fully merged into Pakistan in 1955.
